title: Harassment response foundations
summary: Learn how to spot harassment patterns, document incidents safely, and choose the right escalation path without increasing harm.
outcomes: Identify verbal, digital, and power-based forms of harassment.
Separate facts, evidence, and assumptions while documenting incidents.
Choose between internal reporting, official channels, and urgent emergency support.

lessons.title: Recognize unsafe behavior
points: Harassment can be repeated or one-off if the impact is serious enough.
Power differences matter: manager-employee, senior-junior, teacher-student, or group pressure.
Digital behavior counts when it intimidates, pressures, or humiliates someone.

lessons.title: Document safely
points: Record date, time, location, people present, exact words or actions, and immediate impact.
Save screenshots, messages, emails, and call logs without editing originals.
Do not pressure a harmed person to retell events repeatedly.

lessons.title: Choose the next action
points: Use emergency services for immediate danger.
Use organizational channels when there is a clear reporting mechanism.
Use official public reporting channels when internal routes are unsafe or unavailable.

quiz.question: What should be captured first in a basic incident record?
options: Facts such as date, time, place, and what happened
quiz.explanation: Start with facts, timing, location, and observed behavior.

quiz.question: If someone is in immediate danger, what comes first?
options: Only save the issue for later
quiz.explanation: Emergency risk should be routed immediately to urgent response channels.

quiz.question: Why is evidence preservation important?
options: It reduces confusion and supports reporting
quiz.explanation: Evidence helps clarify events but does not replace support or guarantee outcomes.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz

title: Consent and healthy boundaries
summary: Turn consent into practical communication habits for in-person and digital interactions.
outcomes: Explain consent as informed, specific, freely given, and reversible.
Recognize pressure, guilt, silence, and imbalance as warning signs.
Use respectful boundary-setting language in real situations.

lessons.title: Define consent clearly
points: Consent is an active and informed yes, not the absence of a no.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time.
A yes to one action does not mean yes to everything.

lessons.title: Spot pressure patterns
points: Silence under pressure is not enthusiastic agreement.
Repeated asking after a refusal is pressure, not healthy communication.
Sharing private images without permission is a serious boundary violation.

lessons.title: Practice boundary language
points: Use simple direct statements: I am not comfortable with that.
Give young people language that is clear and repeatable.
Support the person who set the boundary instead of challenging them.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects consent?
options: Consent can be withdrawn at any time
Pressure is acceptable if the relationship is close
quiz.explanation: Consent must remain voluntary and can always be withdrawn.

quiz.question: A repeated request after someone says no is:
options: A private issue that never matters
quiz.explanation: Repeated asking after refusal is pressure.

quiz.question: What helps create healthier boundaries?
quiz.explanation: Clear direct communication lowers confusion and pressure.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz

title: Digital safety and scam defense
summary: Protect accounts, spot scams faster, and respond quickly to cyber abuse or fraud.
outcomes: Recognize phishing, impersonation, sextortion, and device takeover patterns.
Use password hygiene, account recovery tools, and privacy settings correctly.
Know when to use 1930 and the cybercrime portal.

lessons.title: Protect key accounts
points: Use a password manager and unique passwords where possible.
Enable two-factor authentication for email, banking, and social accounts.
Review recovery email and phone details regularly.

lessons.title: Spot common scam patterns
points: Urgent requests, payment pressure, and fake authority are common red flags.
Shortened links and spoofed contact names are often used in phishing attacks.
Do not send money or private images under digital pressure.

lessons.title: Respond after compromise
points: Change credentials from a trusted device.
Preserve screenshots and transaction details.
Use official reporting channels quickly when financial fraud is involved.

quiz.question: Which sign is a common phishing indicator?
options: Unexpected urgency and a suspicious link
quiz.explanation: Urgency plus suspicious links is a classic phishing pattern.

quiz.question: What should you do after account compromise?
quiz.explanation: Credential reset and evidence preservation are the immediate priorities.

quiz.question: 1930 is most relevant for:
options: Cyber fraud and urgent digital financial response
quiz.explanation: 1930 is used for urgent cyber fraud support and reporting flow.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz

title: Mental health first response
summary: Use calm, non-judgmental first-response language and route people toward appropriate support.
outcomes: Respond without diagnosing or minimizing someone else's distress.
Identify when a situation may need urgent or professional support.
Use referral language that is supportive and respectful.

lessons.title: Start with safety and calm
points: Use short, calm phrases and avoid judgment.
Check for immediate risk when someone sounds unsafe or overwhelmed.
Do not promise secrecy if urgent danger is involved.

lessons.title: Listen without fixing everything
points: Listening is not the same as taking over the entire problem.
Reflect back what you heard and ask what support feels useful.
Do not force advice or timelines on the person.

lessons.title: Refer when needed
points: Use professional or official support when risk, self-harm, or persistent distress is present.
Tele-MANAS can be one support route for mental-health-related help.
Document urgent concerns if your setting has a safeguarding process.

quiz.question: What is a better first response to distress?
quiz.explanation: Calm listening and checking safety is the appropriate first step.

quiz.question: When should secrecy not be promised?
quiz.explanation: Urgent safety issues may require escalation and support from others.

quiz.question: What is the goal of referral?
options: To pass people off without care
To connect them with appropriate support
quiz.explanation: Referral is about connecting people to appropriate help.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz

title: Reporting, documentation, and referrals
summary: Build a repeatable process for incident logging, referrals, internal follow-up, and official reporting.
outcomes: Create consistent incident records without over-collecting information.
Track status and next actions clearly.
Reduce delays between disclosure, support, and referral.

lessons.title: Create a lean incident log
points: Capture what happened, who was involved, and what immediate support was requested.
Use neutral language and avoid speculation.
Track where the case was referred and who owns the next action.

lessons.title: Manage follow-up
points: Assign an owner, next checkpoint, and current status.
Do not let serious issues disappear into informal chat threads.
Respect confidentiality while keeping action visible to the right people.

lessons.title: Know official routes
points: Use 112 for immediate emergency risk.
Use official cybercrime and women's channels when relevant.
Use institutional routes only if they are safe and functional.

quiz.question: What makes an incident log useful?
options: Neutral facts and clear next actions
quiz.explanation: A useful record captures facts and the next step.

quiz.question: Why assign an owner to follow-up?
options: To make the issue look closed

quiz.question: Which route comes first in immediate danger?
quiz.explanation: Immediate safety issues should go to emergency response.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz

title: Bystander leadership and community safety
summary: Build safer intervention habits that balance courage, personal safety, and group responsibility.
outcomes: Choose between direct intervention, distraction, delegation, documentation, and delayed support.
Understand when not to intervene alone.
Translate one-off workshops into community norms and follow-up routines.

lessons.title: Choose the right intervention style
points: Direct action is not always the safest option.
Delegation is powerful when formal authority or backup is needed.
Delayed support still matters if immediate intervention is unsafe.

lessons.title: Protect yourself while helping
points: Intervention should not create new serious harm.
Call for backup when power differences or violence risk are high.
Document and escalate when witnessing digital or public abuse.

lessons.title: Build group habits
points: Set clear behavior norms and reporting reminders in teams or clubs.
Use brief refresher sessions instead of only one annual event.
Review real examples and what the group learned from them.

quiz.question: Which option is part of bystander intervention?
quiz.explanation: Delegation is one of the safer intervention methods.

quiz.question: When should you avoid intervening alone?
options: When violence or serious escalation risk is high
When a problem is small enough to ignore forever
quiz.explanation: High-risk situations may require backup or formal channels.

quiz.question: What makes a workshop culture stick?
quiz.explanation: Repetition and follow-up turn awareness into culture.

completion_criteria: Score 70% or higher on the quiz
